lead: Both readings are about belonging to Christ when it costs something. Paul has every right to be supported by the Corinthians, yet he gives up that right so that nothing may hinder the Gospel. In John, many disciples leave Jesus after his teaching on the bread of life, and Peter, speaking for the Twelve, stays: “Lord, to whom can we go?” In the Season of the Apostles the Church learns from both: an apostle holds his rights loosely and holds on to Christ.

set: Paul has just told the Corinthians to give up eating food offered to idols if it would make a weaker brother fall (8:13). Now he shows that he lives by the same rule. Some at Corinth questioned whether he was truly an apostle, perhaps because he worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3) and refused their money. He answers that he has all the rights of an apostle, and has chosen not to use them.
str: vv. 1–2: Paul’s credentials: he has seen the Lord, and the Corinthians themselves are the seal of his apostleship.
vv. 3–6: the rights of an apostle: food and drink, a companion, freedom from manual work.
vv. 7–10: proofs from daily life (soldier, vinedresser, shepherd) and from the law of Moses.
vv. 11–12: the conclusion: he has the right, but he has not used it, for the sake of the Gospel.
kw: One who is sent with the authority of the sender. For Paul an apostle must have seen the Risen Lord (15:8) and been sent by him. That is why his first proof is: “Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?”
The mark pressed into wax to show that a document is genuine. The faith of the Corinthians is the Lord’s own stamp on Paul’s work.
The word runs through the whole chapter. Paul does not deny his rights; he shows that love may lay them down. The same freedom marks his Master, who “emptied himself” (Philippians 2:7).
vv: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?
Paul saw the Risen Lord on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6). His freedom is not freedom from service but freedom for it.
Do we not have the right to be accompanied by a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?

The Greek says literally “a sister, a wife”. Many read it of the apostles’ wives, and Peter was married (Mark 1:30). Some Fathers, among them St Jerome, read it of devout women who served the apostles, as women served Jesus (Luke 8:3). On “the brothers of the Lord”, see the question below.
You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 25:4. The law that cared for the working ox teaches, all the more, care for the one who labours for the Gospel.
Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
This is the heart of the passage. The Gospel must never seem to be for sale.
ch: The Church has always taught both halves of this reading: the faithful should support those who serve them in the Gospel (see Luke 10:7; Code of Canon Law, canon 222), and those who serve should not seek gain. The Second Vatican Council asks priests to use goods only for their right purposes and to embrace a voluntary poverty that makes them more like Christ (Presbyterorum Ordinis 17). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, praises Paul for going beyond what was commanded, taking no wages where he could have taken them (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians).

set: The long discourse in the synagogue at Capernaum is over (6:59). Jesus has said that he is the bread of life and that his flesh must be eaten and his blood drunk. Many who followed him find it too hard (6:60). These verses tell the result: a great falling away, and a small, firm confession of faith from the Twelve. John’s Gospel has no scene at Caesarea Philippi; this is its counterpart, Peter’s confession.
str: vv. 64–65: Jesus knows who do not believe; no one comes unless the Father grants it.
v. 67: the question to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?”
vv. 68–69: Peter’s answer: the words of eternal life; the Holy One of God.
vv. 70–71: yet one of the chosen Twelve will betray him.
kw: A rare title, used elsewhere by an unclean spirit who knows who Jesus is (Mark 1:24). Peter confesses that Jesus belongs wholly to God and comes from him.
we have come to believe and know
Both verbs are in the Greek perfect tense: a faith begun in the past that still stands. In John, believing and knowing go together; faith is a way of knowing.
Literally “slanderer, one who sets apart”. Jesus does not say Judas was created evil. He was chosen and loved, and he let the adversary enter his heart (13:2, 27).
vv: Because of this many of his disciples turned back and no longer went about with him.
It is worth noticing that Jesus does not run after them to soften his words. He does not trade the truth of the Eucharist for numbers.
So Jesus asked the twelve, “Do you also wish to go away?”
The question respects their freedom. Love that forces is not love.
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not say he has understood everything. He says there is no one else. Trust comes before full understanding.
ch: The Catechism recalls this scene when it speaks of the Eucharist: the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them, and the Lord’s question “Will you also go away?” echoes through the ages as an invitation to discover that only he has the words of eternal life, and that to receive the gift of his Eucharist in faith is to receive the Lord himself (CCC 1336). St Augustine, preaching on this passage, admires Peter’s answer: he speaks for the Twelve, and he puts believing before knowing; we believe so that we may know (in substance, Tractates on John 27).

qa: Paul speaks of “the brothers of the Lord”. Did Jesus have brothers?

The Church has always believed that Mary remained a virgin. In Hebrew and Aramaic, and in the Bible’s Greek, “brother” is used for close relatives such as cousins (in the Hebrew of Genesis 13:8 Abram calls his nephew Lot his brother; NRSV kindred). James and Joseph, called brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55), are sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). The Catechism explains that these are close relations of Jesus, according to an Old Testament way of speaking (CCC 500).
study: Paul gave up a right so that the Gospel would not be hindered. Is there a right or comfort I could lay down for the sake of someone’s faith?
When Christ’s teaching is hard for me, what helps me to say with Peter, “Lord, to whom can we go?”
